query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultrathin, nanostructured, gradient tribo-coating on a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will provide adaptive tribological protection, yielding a consistently lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate from room temperature to 800 °C under varying loads and environmental conditions compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix without special surface modifications, which shows difficulty in maintaining low friction and wear across a wide temperature range.
generation.intervention: Design and deposition of an ultrathin, nanostructured, gradient tribo-coating that is engineered to adapt its properties with temperature.
generation.conditions: Sliding tribotesting conducted from room temperature to 800 °C with systematic variations in applied load (low to high) and environmental conditions (e.g., ambient air and inert atmospheres).
generation.structural_mediator: A gradient tribo-layer that, at low temperatures, maintains metallic bonding and low shear resistance and, at high temperatures, undergoes controlled oxidation to form a stable, lubricious glaze layer with nanocrystalline features.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the engineered coating acts as a low-shear interface that diminishes adhesive wear. As temperature increases, controlled tribo-oxidation within the gradient structure initiates the formation of a nanocrystalline glaze layer that minimizes both adhesive and oxidative wear by providing a protective barrier and adapting to strain gradients.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the starting CoCrFeNi alloy, the coated sample will exhibit a reduction in friction coefficient and specific wear rate consistently across the 25 °C to 800 °C range, even under variable loads and in oxidizing environments.
generation.baseline: Unmodified CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy, which tends to have higher friction and wear rate due to failure in adapting its surface characteristics over the full temperature range.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under sliding conditions spanning room temperature to 800 °C, across varying normal loads (from low to high) and in both oxidizing (ambient air) and inert environments. Its performance might be limited if the reactive kinetics do not sufficiently form the protective glaze at very rapid temperature changes or under extreme load conditions outside the typical testing range.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements (e.g., percentage reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate) are uncertain, and the durability of the adaptive glaze layer under abrupt transitions or prolonged high-load conditions remains to be thoroughly validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy specimens: one set with the deposited gradient nanostructured tribo-coating and one unmodified control set. Perform sliding tribotesting over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C while systematically varying normal load and environmental conditions (ambient air vs. inert gas).
measurements: Coefficient of friction across the temperature range
Wear rate (mm3/Nm) determined through wear volume measurements
Surface and cross-sectional morphology (to verify formation and integrity of the glaze layer) via SEM/TEM
Phase/chemical composition changes on the sliding surface using XPS or Raman spectroscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the gradient tribo-coated specimens do not demonstrate a statistically significant and consistent reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate relative to the unmodified alloy across the entire temperature range and under varied load and environmental conditions, or if the expected adaptive formation of the lubricious glaze layer is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 3A shows the Vickers hardness and wear rate variations of NiX and Ni3X as the temperature increases from RT to 800 °C. The hardness of NiX and Ni3X gradually decreases from 6.1 GPa and 4.3 GPa at RT to 3.7 GPa and 2.5 GPa at 800 °C, respectively. The high thermal hardness of NiX arises from the solid solution strengthening and the resultant heterostructures [,]. The trend in wear rate of the Ni3X with temperature is similar to that of the conventional alloys. Specifically, its wear rate increases from 1.1 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at RT to 4.2 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at 600 °C, but decreases afterward to 2.4 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at 800 °C. However, the wear rate of the NiX is basically maintained at the order of (10−7 to 10−6) mm3/Nm over the entire test temperature. In particular, it achieves ultra-low wear at RT (1.7 × 10−7 mm3/Nm) and 800 °C (9.1 × 10−7 mm3/Nm). In the present study, the tribological properties of different grain sizes CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were systematically analyzed based on sliding experiments and worn surface morphology characterization under different sliding speeds and normal loads. The results can be summarized as follows: Under the normal low load and low sliding speed, the main wear mechanism of FG and CG samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. However, the material of CG is easy to soften under the action of friction heat during high sliding speed, and the oxide layer formed is easy to fracture. Under the normal high load, the wear mechanisms of FG and CG samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation with the increase of sliding speed. The oxidation layer formed on CG sample has many cracks, and the wear surface of CG sample also has plastic deformation, resulting in an increase in friction coefficient and specific wear rate and a decrease in wear resistance. Therefore, under high load and low load, FG sample has good wear resistance due to its high surface strength.

decision.trend: Early studies evolved from alloying adjustments (e.g., W additions in AlCoCrFeNiWx) that promoted the formation of secondary phases to improve high‐temperature wear resistance, to investigations on grain size and dynamic nanostructuring (as seen in studies on inverse Hall–Petch behavior and nanohierarchical architectures) that foster the formation of adaptive near-surface layers. In these works, researchers first targeted modifications to the bulk composition to stabilize intermetallic or finely dispersed phases at elevated temperatures, then moved to designing engineered surface architectures that generate in situ protective glaze layers during sliding. Although these approaches yielded low friction or wear improvements in subsets of the operating conditions, none provided a single, unified intervention to ensure robust, low friction and wear performance across the entire room temperature–800 °C regime under variable loads and environments.
decision.unsolved: The challenge remains to achieve a single, reliable modification for the CoCrFeNi matrix that continuously regulates the tribological response over the full temperature range, bridging the differences between low-temperature adhesive wear and high-temperature oxidative/plasticity‐driven wear mechanisms while also withstanding variations in load and ambient conditions.
decision.lever: Design and deposition of an ultrathin, nanostructured, gradient tribo-coating that is engineered to be adaptive: it forms a stable, in situ glaze layer at high temperatures (driven by controlled oxidation/reaction kinetics) while maintaining metallic bonding and low shear resistance at lower temperatures.
decision.why: This approach naturally follows the trend from bulk alloying and microstructural refinement toward tailoring the near-surface architecture. Previous studies demonstrated that adaptive, nanohierarchical interfaces lower friction and improve wear by dynamically counterbalancing different wear mechanisms. Engineering a gradient surface layer specifically targets the performance limitations and the open question for CoCrFeNi by providing a single intervention that adjusts its lubricious behavior as temperature, load, and environment vary.
